```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
library(varm)
set.seed(42)
y <- as.matrix(yraw)
colnames(y) <- c("inflation", "unemployment", "rate")
fit <- varm(y, p = 2)
```

Reduced-form innovations satisfy $u_t = P\varepsilon_t$ with
$PP' = \Sigma$. An identification scheme chooses $P$. Each `id_*()`
constructor returns a small specification object passed to the `id` argument
of `irf()`, `fevd()` and `hd()`, for both `varm` and `bvarm` fits.

Implemented: `id_chol()`, `id_longrun()`, `id_sign()`, `id_given()`.
Proxy/external-instrument SVAR is covered in the last section.

## Cholesky (recursive)

The first variable in `order` is the most exogenous. Variables can be given
by name.

```{r chol}
ir1 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, nboot = 200)
ir2 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(order = c("rate", "inflation", "unemployment")),
           horizon = 12, ci = "none")
round(ir1$estimate[, , 1], 3)   # impact matrix P (response x shock)
```

```{r chol-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(ir1)
```

## Long-run restrictions (Blanchard-Quah)

The cumulative long-run response matrix is restricted to be lower
triangular, so the second shock has no long-run effect on the first variable,
and so on. Variables should be stationary growth rates or differences, and
the ordering is the column order of the data. Here we use the sample
series purely to show the mechanics.

```{r longrun}
ir_lr <- irf(fit, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 40, ci = "none")
ir_lr
# long-run effect: cumulative responses over a long horizon are lower triangular
ir_long <- irf(fit, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 2000, ci = "none")
round(apply(ir_long$estimate, c(1, 2), sum), 2)
```

Use `cumulative = "unemployment"` in `irf()` to accumulate the response of a
differenced variable into a level response.

## Sign restrictions

`restrictions` is a $K \times K$ matrix (rows: variables, columns: shocks)
with entries `+1`, `-1` or `0` (unrestricted). A matrix is imposed over
`horizon` periods from impact; a $K \times K \times H$ array gives
horizon-specific restrictions. Draws use Haar-distributed rotations of the
Cholesky factor (Rubio-Ramirez, Waggoner and Zha, 2010); `nrot` accepted
rotations are kept per reduced-form draw, up to `maxtry` attempts. Only sign
restrictions are supported; zero restrictions are not.

A stylised monetary-policy shock: the rate rises, inflation does not rise.
The other two shocks are left unrestricted.

```{r sign}
S <- matrix(0, 3, 3, dimnames = list(c("inflation", "unemployment", "rate"),
                                     c("mp", "s2", "s3")))
S["rate", "mp"] <- 1
S["inflation", "mp"] <- -1
id_sign(S, horizon = 2)   # printing an id object shows the restrictions
ir_sign <- irf(fit, id = id_sign(S, horizon = 2, nrot = 5, maxtry = 5000),
               horizon = 16, nboot = 100)
ir_sign
```

The `estimate` is the median across accepted rotations; for `varm` fits the
sample-based set estimate is stored in `$set_estimate`. The acceptance rate
is `ir_sign$accept_rate`. If no draw satisfies the restrictions, `irf()`
stops with an error. Sign restrictions identify a set, so the pointwise
median is not one coherent model; `hd()` for a `varm` fit uses the first
accepted rotation at the point estimate.

```{r sign-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(ir_sign, shocks = 1)
```

## User-supplied impact matrix

`id_given(P)` takes any $P$ with $PP' = \Sigma$ and does not check this.

```{r given}
P <- t(chol(fit$Sigma))
ir_g <- irf(fit, id = id_given(P), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
all.equal(unname(ir_g$estimate[, , 1]), unname(P))
```

## Using identification elsewhere

```{r other}
fv <- fevd(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "none")
h  <- hd(fit, id = id_chol())
```

## Proxy SVAR and weak-instrument-robust sets

`varm_proxy()` identifies one shock with an external instrument $m_t$ (Mertens-Ravn, Stock-Watson):
the impact vector is proportional to $\Gamma = E[u_t m_t]$, normalised so the `target` variable moves by `size`.
Wild-bootstrap bands are unreliable when the instrument is weak, so `varm_proxy_robust()` computes the
Montiel Olea-Stock-Watson (2021) Anderson-Rubin-type confidence sets, valid at any instrument strength.
Each set is bounded (`case` 1), the complement of an interval (2), empty (3) or the whole line (4);
unbounded sets are reported as `-Inf`/`Inf` and empty ones as `NA`. `proxy_fstat()` reports the
HAC Wald first-stage statistic `F_hac` that governs which case to expect.

```{r proxy}
set.seed(1)
e <- matrix(rnorm(600), 300)
y <- matrix(0, 300, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("y1", "y2")))
for (t in 2:300) y[t, ] <- 0.5 * y[t - 1, ] + c(e[t, 1] + 0.3 * e[t, 2], e[t, 2] + 0.5 * e[t, 1])
pfit <- varm(y, p = 1)
m <- e[, 1] + rnorm(300, sd = 0.5)            # relevant instrument for shock 1
proxy_fstat(pfit, m)
rb <- varm_proxy_robust(pfit, m, horizon = 6, level = c(0.68, 0.90))
rb
round(cbind(est = rb$estimate[, "y2"], lower = rb$lower[, "y2", 2], upper = rb$upper[, "y2", 2]), 3)

# a pure-noise instrument: the sets become unbounded
varm_proxy_robust(pfit, rnorm(300), horizon = 3, level = 0.9)$case[, , 1]
```

## Not yet implemented

Identification through
heteroskedasticity, zero restrictions and narrative sign restrictions,
Bayesian sampling of the rotation with a prior on $Q$ beyond uniform Haar,
and non-Gaussian identification.
